question:
What is the minimum number of small squares that must be shaded so that a line of symmetry lies on the diagonal \(\overline{BD}\) of square \(ABCD\)?

[Figure 1](figures/2005_AMC_8_Q03_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
Imagine folding the square along \(BD\). For symmetry, every shaded square must land on another shaded square. Number the rows from top to bottom and the columns from left to right, starting with 1.

The shaded squares in row 1, columns 1 and 3, reflect to row 4, column 4 and row 2, column 4, respectively. The shaded square in row 3, column 4 reflects to row 1, column 2. The shaded square in row 4, column 2 reflects to row 3, column 1. The remaining shaded square, at the top right, reflects onto itself.

The four reflected partners just identified are distinct and currently unshaded, so all four must be shaded. After those additions, every shaded square has a shaded reflected partner, giving symmetry across \(BD\). Thus the minimum is \(\boxed{4}\), choice \(\mathrm{D}\).
